articles.author: Hommer
articles.description:
If you've ever copied photos off an iPhone and found a folder full of .heic files, you're not alone. Since iOS 11, iPhones save photos in HEIC (High Efficiency Image Container, part of the HEIF standard) by default. It keeps good quality at roughly half the size of a JPG, which is great for phone storage, but plenty of Windows apps, upload forms and print services still won't accept it.
Here are three practical ways to get JPGs out of them.
Settings > Camera > Formats > Most Compatible makes the camera shoot JPG from now on. Files get bigger, and it doesn't touch photos you've already taken.
Settings > Photos > Transfer to Mac or PC > Automatic converts photos to a compatible format when you copy them over a cable.
macOS: open the file in Preview and choose File > Export > JPEG, or select several files in Finder and use Quick Actions > Convert Image. From the terminal: sips -s format jpeg in.heic --out out.jpg.
Windows 10/11: install HEIF Image Extensions from the Microsoft Store (some files also need HEVC Video Extensions), then open the photo in Paint and use Save as > JPEG.
Linux: heif-convert in.heic out.jpg from the libheif-examples package, or ImageMagick built with libheif.
When you're on a machine you can't install things on, a browser-based converter is the quickest route. I built Convert HEIC to JPG for this: you drop in one or many .heic files and download JPGs. The decoding runs in your browser, so the photos aren't uploaded to a server. It's free, needs no signup, accepts files up to 50MB and can also output PNG or WebP.
If you mostly share photos with Windows users, switching the camera to Most Compatible saves the most hassle. For a one-off batch, the built-in Mac tools or a browser converter are the fastest. For scripts and servers, libheif or ImageMagick is the way to go.
articles.title: Why your iPhone photos are .heic files, and three ways to get JPGs

Avoiding stale and cross-provider reference data in financial destination flows.
Bank lists are ideal cache candidates. They are requested frequently, can be large, and usually change less often than transaction data.
They are also easy to cache incorrectly.
When a platform supports multiple payout providers, each provider may use its own bank identifiers, names, availability rules, and supported institutions. A shared bank-list cache can serve valid data from the wrong rail.
At minimum, the cache key should include:
country
provider
directory version

articles.description:
Preventing duplicate customer messages when background jobs retry.
Push notifications are not financial ledger entries, but duplicates still damage trust. A customer should not receive the same failure alert three times because a worker retried, nor should two scheduler processes send the same campaign simultaneously.
Task queues normally provide at-least-once execution. Notification systems must design around that fact.
Two workers can pick up the same scheduled campaign. Reading its status and then updating it is vulnerable to a race.
Lock the campaign and transition it to sending inside one database transaction:
with database_transaction():
    campaign = Campaign.objects.select_for_update().get(id=campaign_id)

    if campaign.status not in {"draft", "queued", "scheduled"}:
        ret…

articles.description: The article analyzes the relationship between human identity and artificial intelligence systems, introducing a key distinction between the essential self, the nominalized subject, and the simulated subject. The author warns against the process of outsourcing thought (nominalization), which leads to the loss of real human agency, and against the anthropomorphization of AI systems that merely imitate human behavior. It is emphasized that precise modeling of style and data is not equivalent to personal continuity or possessing phenomenal consciousness. In the face of the development of AI agents, it becomes crucial to distinguish between a person and their digital model in order to maintain intellectual sovereignty and biographical authenticity in a world increasingly dominated by simulations.

articles.author: Soumyajit Mukherjee
articles.description:
HTTP status codes are more than numbers.
They communicate what happened during an HTTP request.
Using them consistently makes APIs easier to consume and debug.
A common example:
200 OK

means the request succeeded.
Another important status is:
201 Created

which is useful when a resource has been created.
For example:
POST /users

might return:
201 Created

These usually indicate that something about the request isn't acceptable.
Examples:
400 Bad Request
401 Unauthorized
403 Forbidden
404 Not Found
409 Conflict
429 Too Many Requests

For example, an unauthenticated request might receive:
401 Unauthorized

while an authenticated user lacking permission may receive:
403 Forbidden

These indicate that the server encountered an error.
The classic example:
500 Internal Server Error

Another useful code is:
503 Service Unavailable

which can indicate temporary service unavailability.
Imagine an API that returns:
200

for every request, even when something fails.
The client now has to inspect custom fields to determine whether the operation succeeded.
Standard HTTP semantics make APIs much easier to understand.
You don't need to memorize every status code.
Start with:
200
201
204
400
401
403
404
409
429
500
503

These cover a large portion of everyday API development.
Good API design isn't only about endpoints and JSON.
The status codes are part of the API contract too.
articles.title: How HTTP Status Codes Make APIs Easier to Understand

articles.author: The Block Research
articles.description:
Layer 2 scaling solutions help blockchains like Ethereum process more activity without forcing every transaction to happen directly on the base chain.
Ethereum’s main network is secure and decentralized, but blockspace is limited. When demand rises, fees increase and users can get priced out. Layer 2s address this by moving transaction activity to scaling systems that sit around Ethereum while still using it for settlement, security, data posting, or verification.
The most important Layer 2 designs today are rollups. Rollups process transactions off-chain, bundle them together, and post data or proofs back to Ethereum. This makes transactions cheaper and faster while keeping a connection to Ethereum’s trust foundation.
articles.title: Layer 2 Scaling Solutions
